Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- Robert Barnett, a prominent Washington attorney, has worked on eight national presidential campaigns, focusing on debate preparation. He played the role of George H.W. Bush in practice debates with Geraldine Ferraro in 1984 and with Michael Dukakis in 1988, and practice debated Bill Clinton more than 20 times during the 1992 campaign. He also played the role of Dick Cheney in 2000 and 2004 and helped prepare Hillary Clinton for 23 primary debates for the 2008 nomination. Barnett spoke with CNNI's Michael Holmes. Robert Barnett has been in practice debates with Democrats from Geraldine Ferraro to Bill Clinton. CNN: How does Tuesday night's town hall format differ from other debates? Barnett: The individuals will not necessarily express the question as a journalist would. So, for example, one of these people will probably not ask about Internal Revenue Service Code section 341, but rather will ask about their taxes and their tax burdens and what they care about with respect to taxation. And so you have to be very careful to be sure you understand what the individual is asking about and you have to be particularly careful to answer the question, because if you don't, you risk alienating the questioner and the audience and the listeners. CNN: You're in a unique position. You have prepped, I think, seven or eight presidential campaigns. You've done debate prep, you've stood in and played the role of Dick Cheney and others. What's that like? What are you trying to do to prepare the candidate, any candidate? Barnett:  If I'm playing the surrogate, if you will, if I'm the Republican for a Democrat, I try to prepare myself -- not to imitate; I'm not Darrell Hammond or Dana Carvey. I'm not that talented. But I try to be ready with what my candidate that I'm playing, if you will, has said -- the exact words used, the way they counterattack, the way they attack. And I try to make sure that the candidate I'm working with, meaning the Democrat, has heard just about everything that they could hear from their opponent before they ever walk on the stage. CNN: Do you try to bait them, get them to bite a little and then say that's not what you should be doing? Barnett: Well, it can get pretty contested. When I prepared with Rep. Geraldine Ferraro in 1984 when she was running against then-vice president George Herbert Walker Bush, I baited her a lot and she got so angry with me that she frequently walked over to me and slugged me on the arm. So I left the process black and blue. CNN: When you're doing that sort of thing, how direct can you be with the candidate? Or do you have to treat them with a bit of kid gloves? Barnett: I treat them with no kid gloves. It's fair to say I'm direct, I make sure they hear everything from me before they hear it on the stage and maybe hear it even a little more aggressively so they can be prepared.

**(CNN) —** Robert Barnett, a prominent Washington attorney, has worked on eight national presidential campaigns, specializing in debate preparation. He portrayed George H.W. Bush in practice debates with Geraldine Ferraro in 1984 and Michael Dukakis in 1988, and participated in more than 20 practice debates with Bill Clinton during the 1992 campaign. He also played the role of Dick Cheney in 2000 and 2004 and helped prepare Hillary Clinton for 23 primary debates during her campaign for the 2008 nomination.

Barnett spoke with CNN International’s Michael Holmes. He has participated in practice debates with Democrats ranging from Geraldine Ferraro to Bill Clinton.

**CNN: How does Tuesday night’s town hall format differ from other debates?**

**Barnett:** The individuals will not necessarily phrase their questions as a journalist would. For example, one of them probably will not ask about Internal Revenue Service Code Section 341, but instead will ask about their taxes, their tax burdens and the aspects of taxation that matter to them.

You therefore have to be very careful to ensure that you understand what the individual is asking. You must also take particular care to answer the question, because if you do not, you risk alienating the questioner, the audience and the listeners.

**CNN: You’re in a unique position. You have prepared candidates for, I think, seven or eight presidential campaigns. You’ve conducted debate preparation and stood in for Dick Cheney and others. What is that like? What are you trying to do to prepare a candidate—any candidate?**

**Barnett:** If I’m playing the surrogate—if I’m portraying the Republican opponent for a Democrat—I prepare myself not to imitate the person; I’m not Darrell Hammond or Dana Carvey. I’m not that talented.

But I do try to familiarize myself with what the candidate I’m portraying has said: the exact words used, the way the candidate counterattacks and the way the candidate attacks. I try to ensure that the candidate I’m working with—meaning the Democrat—has heard nearly everything the opponent might say before ever walking onto the stage.

**CNN: Do you try to bait candidates—to get them to take the bait—and then tell them that’s not what they should be doing?**

**Barnett:** It can become quite contentious. When I prepared with Rep. Geraldine Ferraro in 1984, when she was running against then–Vice President George Herbert Walker Bush, I baited her frequently. She became so angry with me that she often walked over and punched me in the arm. I left the process black and blue.

**CNN: When you’re doing that sort of work, how direct can you be with the candidate? Or do you have to treat the candidate with kid gloves?**

**Barnett:** I do not use kid gloves. It is fair to say that I’m direct. I make sure candidates hear everything from me before they hear it onstage—and perhaps hear it delivered even a little more aggressively—so that they can be prepared.

**(CNN) —** Robert Barnett, a well-known Washington lawyer, has participated in debate training for eight presidential campaigns. In 1984, he portrayed George H.W. Bush during Geraldine Ferraro’s rehearsal sessions, then took on the same role while preparing Michael Dukakis in 1988. During the 1992 race, Barnett held more than 20 mock debates with Bill Clinton. He later stood in as Dick Cheney in both 2000 and 2004 and assisted Hillary Clinton as she prepared for 23 primary debates during her 2008 nomination campaign.

Barnett discussed his experiences with CNN International’s Michael Holmes. His mock-debate work with Democrats has ranged from Ferraro to Clinton.

**CNN:** What distinguishes Tuesday evening’s town hall from other types of debates?

**Barnett:** Members of the public may frame issues differently from professional reporters. Someone probably will not pose a question about Section 341 of the Internal Revenue Service Code, for instance. Instead, that person is more likely to talk about personal taxes, the burden they face, and the tax concerns that matter to them. Candidates therefore need to listen closely, understand what the person truly wants to know, and respond directly. Failing to do so could turn off the person asking the question, as well as the wider audience and those listening elsewhere.

**CNN:** You bring unusual experience to this process. You have helped prepare candidates in, I believe, seven or eight presidential campaigns, and you have portrayed figures including Dick Cheney during rehearsals. What does that involve, and what are you seeking to accomplish for a candidate?

**Barnett:** When I serve as the opponent’s stand-in—such as representing a Republican while helping a Democrat—I do not attempt a theatrical impersonation. I am neither Darrell Hammond nor Dana Carvey, and I do not have their abilities. My goal is to thoroughly study the person I am portraying: the precise language that candidate has used, the person’s offensive tactics, and how they respond to attacks. I want the Democrat I am assisting to encounter nearly every argument or line of criticism the real opponent might use before stepping onto the debate stage.

**CNN:** Do you deliberately provoke candidates to see whether they react, then explain that they should avoid responding that way?

**Barnett:** The rehearsals can become quite confrontational. In 1984, when I worked with Representative Geraldine Ferraro as she campaigned against Vice President George Herbert Walker Bush, I repeatedly tried to provoke her. She became so furious that she often came over and punched me in the arm. By the end of the preparation process, I was covered in bruises.

**CNN:** In those circumstances, how frank can you be? Must you handle candidates gently?

**Barnett:** I do not handle them gently at all. I am very straightforward. I want them to hear every possible challenge from me before facing it in the actual debate—and I may deliver it even more forcefully during practice so they will be ready.

Veteran debate coach Robert Barnett describes town hall debate preparation as a demanding exercise in anticipation, discipline, and empathy. Candidates rehearse with stand-ins who study their opponents closely and attempt to reproduce not only their positions and familiar lines, but also their likely attacks, interruptions, and counterattacks. The goal is to make the practice sessions as realistic as possible so that the candidate is prepared to respond calmly and effectively under pressure.

These rehearsals are not limited to memorizing facts or polishing short answers. Surrogates challenge candidates from multiple angles, forcing them to defend their records, explain policy differences, and handle unexpected criticism. By repeatedly confronting arguments that are likely to arise during the debate, candidates can identify weak responses, refine their language, and become more comfortable addressing difficult subjects without appearing overly scripted.

Town hall debates present an additional challenge because the questions come from voters rather than solely from moderators. Barnett stresses that candidates must listen closely and understand what each person is truly asking. A question about health care, employment, education, or military service may be rooted in a deeply personal experience. Before turning to a broader policy argument, the candidate must acknowledge that experience and respond directly to the concern behind it.

Failing to do so can have consequences beyond an awkward exchange. If a candidate avoids the question, delivers a rehearsed talking point, or appears insensitive, the voter may feel ignored or disrespected. Viewers at home can reach the same conclusion, especially if they identify with the questioner’s circumstances. A successful town hall performance therefore depends not only on command of policy and readiness for an opponent’s attacks, but also on the ability to engage voters sincerely, answer their questions clearly, and demonstrate that their concerns have been heard.

counterfactuals.output:
# Inside debate prep: Robert Barnett on playing the opponent — and taking off the “kid gloves”

**Washington CNN —** For decades, Washington attorney Robert Barnett has helped Democratic presidential and vice presidential candidates prepare for high-stakes debates.

His job in mock sessions has often been to portray the Republican opponent: studying the candidate’s arguments, mannerisms and pressure points, then testing the Democrat under conditions designed to feel as uncomfortable as the real event.

In an interview-style discussion, Barnett explained why town halls present special challenges, why a stand-in must be willing to bait the candidate and why gentle rehearsals do little good. The following Q&A has been edited and condensed for clarity.

---

**CNN: What is the purpose of debate preparation?**

**Barnett:** The goal is not to hand a candidate a script. It is to make sure the candidate is ready for the subjects, attacks and unexpected moments that may arise.

A debate is a live event. Candidates must know their positions, recognize the opponent’s likely strategy and remain disciplined when the exchange moves in an unanticipated direction. Preparation should make those moments feel less surprising.

---

**CNN: How do you prepare to play the opposing candidate?**

**Barnett:** You study everything available: speeches, interviews, previous debates, policy positions and habits of presentation.

The stand-in must understand not only what the opponent is likely to say, but how that person might say it. The object is not entertainment or a perfect impersonation. It is to recreate the opponent’s arguments and tactics closely enough that the candidate experiences a realistic rehearsal.

---

**CNN: Are you trying to provoke the candidate during those sessions?**

**Barnett:** Yes. Baiting can be an important part of the exercise.

If the opponent is likely to use a particular attack, interrupt, distort an answer or touch a sensitive subject, the candidate should encounter that pressure before debate night. A rehearsal is the place to discover whether someone takes the bait, becomes defensive or gives an answer that is too long or too heated.

The preparation team can then review what happened and work on a more effective response.

---

**CNN: Does that ever feel too aggressive?**

**Barnett:** Effective preparation cannot be conducted with “kid gloves.”

Everyone in the room is there to help the candidate, but that does not mean making the candidate comfortable. A mock opponent who softens attacks or avoids difficult subjects is not doing the job. The real opponent will not be so accommodating.

The sessions should be demanding while remaining focused on the larger objective: ensuring the candidate performs well when the audience is watching.

---

**CNN: How are town hall debates different from traditional debates?**

**Barnett:** Town halls are especially challenging because candidates are not speaking only to a moderator or directly confronting each other. They are answering voters, often on personal or emotionally charged subjects.

That changes the tone. A candidate must engage respectfully with the questioner, provide a substantive answer and remain aware of the opponent’s presence. The physical setting also matters: where to stand, when to move, how to listen and how to avoid appearing to intrude on another person’s space.

A response that might work in a conventional debate can seem cold or overly political when delivered to a voter describing a personal problem.

---

**CNN: Can a candidate rehearse spontaneity?**

**Barnett:** Preparation cannot predict every question, but it can prepare a candidate to handle different categories of questions and different kinds of pressure.

The candidate can practice listening, identifying the central issue and answering it directly before pivoting to a broader point. The aim is not to create a memorized performance. It is to build enough familiarity and confidence that the candidate can react naturally.

---

**CNN: What makes a mock debate successful?**

**Barnett:** It should expose weaknesses rather than conceal them.

If a candidate is vulnerable to a particular line of attack, struggles to answer concisely or reacts badly when challenged, the team needs to know. Discovering that in private is useful. Discovering it for the first time on national television is not.

The best preparation is serious, realistic and sometimes uncomfortable. That is why the opponent must be played forcefully — and why there is no room for kid gloves.
